flashcards.back: A force that moves something away from you: kicking a ball and shoving a box across a table are pushes.
A force that brings something closer to you: dragging a box towards you and reeling in a kite are pulls.
The rubbing force between surfaces that slide against each other: it pushes back against the sliding and slows things down.
The two ends of a magnet, marked N and S: opposite poles attract and like poles repel.

Magnets grab some metals so strongly that they feel like they grab all of them. Magnets ignore most things: they only pull iron and a few metals. In the animation scene s4 the warning is spelled out in the caption itself - a magnet does not attract every metal - so test each metal instead of trusting the shine.
flashcards.front: A magnet attracts every kind of metal.

flashcards.back: A pull, because the box is brought closer to the child
flashcards.front: A child drags a box towards herself across the floor. Which force is she using?

flashcards.back: They push each other apart and repel

items.answer: No: a magnet only pulls iron and a few metals, and ignores most other metals
items.prompt: A pupil says a magnet will attract any metal object. What is wrong with this idea?

items.answer: Friction is the rubbing force between the block and the rough surface; it pushes back against the slide and slows the block down.
items.prompt: A block slides down a rough slope and slows down. Name the force that slows it and explain how it works.

items.answer: It is a push: the foot pushes the ball away.
items.prompt: Kicking a football: is this a push or a pull? Give the reason.

items.answer: They repel: like poles push each other apart.
items.prompt: In one sentence, say what two magnets do when the north pole of one faces the north pole of the other.
